submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole reads a content noun that names a bounded region or span of a larger whole: an extended physical area - an anatomical region or its covering (pelvis, abdomen, belly, gut, chest, torso, skull, spine, neck, back, waist, flank, jaw, forehead, shin, knee, skin, shell, lining), an area or surface of a building (lobby, hallway, porch, attic, basement, balcony, garage, deck, ceiling, floor, roof), or a stretch of land or water or geographic place (interior, coast, shoreline, harbour, port, pier, dock, prairie, tundra, foothills, canyon, outskirts, capital, Nairobi, the Moon) - or, by the same bounded-span generalisation, an interval of time (half, quarter, period, inning, minute, hour, week, month, year, afternoon, morning, night, noon); it peaks on the noun itself, strongest on the word-final sub-token of multi-token words (pel'vis', footh'ills', Nairo'bi'). It stays at zero on discrete objects, fixtures and their parts (chair, table, box, cup, window, door, handle, page), on distal body parts (hand, finger, foot, eye, ear, hair), on establishments treated as functional entities (office, hotel, museum, school, hospital, market) and on the abstract labels for parts (area, region, zone, district, space, part, section, portion); its negative pole is a diffuse near-zero offset that carries no contrastive class.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The restoration of the old farmhouse began in early spring, when the ground was still too wet for heavy machinery. The crew spent the first week documenting every wall, window and doorway with photographs and measurements, because the preservation office required a record of the original fabric before any material was removed. By the second week the scaffolding was up, and the work settled into a rhythm that would hold for the rest of the season: one team opened a section of the structure, a second team repaired it, and a third followed behind with primer and paint.

The eastern wing proved the most difficult. Its foundation had settled unevenly over the previous century, and the timber frame had racked so badly that several of the original joints could no longer be disassembled without splintering. The carpenters braced the wall from the inside, cut the pegs, and lowered the frame in one piece onto a trolley, which they rolled out into the yard where the light was better. Rebuilding it took eleven days. When the frame went back up, the wall stood true to within a sixteenth of an inch, a tolerance the lead carpenter considered adequate for a building of that age.

Water damage occupied the whole of the next month. Rain had found its way past the flashing at the northern chimney for decades, and the joists beneath the valley of the roof had rotted through in places. The crew replaced three joints and sistered the rest, then laid new boards over the repaired areas so that the surface would accept a finish. A specialist was brought in to treat the remaining timber against beetles, since the older beams showed signs of an infestation that had been active, though limited, for some years. He drilled and injected each beam in turn and left a written schedule for the follow-up.

Money was a constant concern. The trust that owned the property raised funds in stages, and each stage had to be accounted for before the next was released. Receipts were filed in a binder kept on the site, and the project manager spent most Friday afternoons reconciling invoices against the schedule of values. Twice the trust asked for an independent review, and twice the review found the books in order but recommended that purchases be approved in advance rather than reimbursed afterward. This slowed the work a little, though nobody complained much, because the alternative was a delay of months.

By late summer the exterior was finished. The painters had primed and caulked every board and had brushed three coats onto the trim, and the new gutter ran without leaking even under a hard test with a hose. The grounds were graded away from the foundation, and a gravel path was laid from the gate to the side entrance so that visitors would not track mud into the house. With the outside secure, the crew turned their attention to the interior, clearing debris from each level in turn and cataloguing whatever they found. In the attic, beneath a layer of dust and old newspaper, they uncovered a hand-lettered map of the property drawn by a previous owner, and on the floor beside it a box of brass fittings that had evidently been set aside for a repair that never happened. Both were photographed, bagged and sent to the archive, where they remain.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Long-context positive holdout: a procedural restoration passage well over 512 tokens in a genre unlike the examples, with claimed region/span nouns (' interior', ' attic', ' floor', ' roof', ' surface', ' week', ' month') present across the passage, so the hypothesis predicts a peak inside rather than at the opening.
